Located just a short walk along the canyon rim from Bright Angel Lodge, the historic viewpoint building is **Lookout Studio** (also known as The Lookout). 

Designed in 1914 by renowned architect Mary Colter for the Santa Fe Railway and the Fred Harvey Company, Lookout Studio was built directly on the cliff edge using native Kaibab limestone to blend seamlessly into the canyon rim. It features outdoor viewing terraces and indoor viewing areas equipped with high-powered telescopes, alongside a small gift shop. 

A little further west along the Rim Trail towards the Bright Angel Trailhead is another historic viewpoint structure, **Kolb Studio**, the multi-story home and photographic studio built by brothers Emery and Ellsworth Kolb starting in 1904.

The best way to see the bottom of Buckskin Gulch while hiking through the Paria Narrows to or from the White House Trailhead is to take a side trip directly at the **Buckskin Gulch & Paria River Confluence**. 

Located roughly 7 miles down-canyon from the White House Trailhead, the confluence marks the junction where Buckskin Gulch empties into the Paria River. As detailed by [Bearfoot Theory](w1) and [Halfway Anywhere](w2), you can simply drop your heavy backpack at the confluence—or at one of the elevated campsites nearby—and hike upstream into the mouth of Buckskin Gulch as an out-and-back spur.

### Tips for this side trip:
- **Distance & Timing:** Walking just 15 to 30 minutes up Buckskin Gulch gives you an immediate look at its soaring, razor-thin Navajo sandstone corridors and dark, sculpted narrows, which feel distinctly narrower and more dramatic than the main Paria corridor.
- **Conditions & Obstacles:** The lower end of Buckskin Gulch often harbors muddy sediment, log jams, and standing pools of murky water that can range from ankle- to waist- or chest-deep. Turn around whenever conditions exceed your comfort level.
- **Flash Flood Safety:** Because slot canyons offer virtually no escape routes, only enter Buckskin Gulch if the weather forecast is completely clear across the entire drainage area.

[w1] 10 Best Utah Backpacking Trips – Bearfoot Theory
  Hiking the Paria River slot canyon from the White House trailhead, including a side trip into Buckskin Gulch, in the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness Area.
  After leaving from the White House trailhead, the canyon begins narrowing down into its legendary slot, passing between towering red walls of Navajo sandstone. Just after 7 miles, you’ll pass the confluence with Buckskin Gulch with a few campsites near the junction. A side trip up the narrow corridor of Buckskin Gulch is a must-do. This is one of the most beautiful and harrowing slot canyons on Earth! Back in the Paria, you’ll continue south, following the endless twists, turns, and meanders into the ever-deepening and narrowing slot.
[w2] Buckskin Gulch and Paria Canyon – The Ultimate Backpacking Guide | HA
  Hiking the final stretch of Buckskin Gulch to the Paria River Confluence, identifying the first safe campsite, and transitioning into Paria Canyon toward Lees Ferry.
  From here, it's more of the same until just before reaching the **Paria River Confluence**. The canyon will open up significantly, revealing extensive vegetation on the left. You'll also find a sandy hill/ramp/elevated spot that you can hike to the top of. This is the **first safe campsite** encountered when hiking through Buckskin Gulch. There is space for camping up top and a few more spots lower down. I believe there are also a few more camping opportunities just past this on the other side of the stream, but I didn't go up to investigate. When you reach the Paria River Confluence, you can either turn left and head out to **White House Campground** via **White House Trail** or you can continue following the Paria River through Paria Canyon toward Lees Ferry. Once you enter Paria Canyon, the canyon walls slowly begin to spread farther apart. You'll follow the river at first (the river may be dry for the first several miles), but soon you'll have the option of cutting up onto sediment deposits around bends as well. You'll still be crossing the river constantly, so don't have any expectation of making it out with dry feet, but you will leave behind the chest-deep slot canyon pools of muck. If you look in the areas on the inside of the river bends, you'll usually be able to find campsites. If you're planning to filter from the springs, pay attention to where they're marked on the map (the map below shows approximate locations only). The springs are not obvious, marked, or necessarily easy to find; I could only find one.

If you catch it at the right time in the afternoon, the sun beams down creating some great photo opportunities. Around mile 7, you reach the confluence of Buckskin Gulch and the Paria River. Buckskin is very narrow with deeper water and has a lot more obstacles than the Paria Narrows. If you have time, you can hike a little ways up Buckskin Gulch. We spent 20 minutes walking up Buckskin until the water started to too deep.

  (Please forgive the horrible “royalty free music.” Ugh.) Paria Canyon and Buckskin Gulch We hiked 5 days and 4 nights, for a total of a little over 40 miles. We started at the trailhead near Lee’s Ferry in Arizona, and exited “the middle route” of Buckskin Gulch in Utah. There was a trail in some places, and random meandering, bushwhacking, and bouldering in others. We seemingly walked across and through the Paria River over 700 times – it’s honestly probably pretty close to that number! And quicksand is bonkers to walk through. It was unnerving at first, but by the end of the trip I was no longer envisioning the scene from * The Princess Bride* playing out in reality.
[w5] Buckskin Gulch: 7+ Tips & Tricks for Navigating Utah’s Best Slot Canyon — 365atlantatraveler.com
  Options for hiking Buckskin Gulch range from day trips to multi-day backpacking permits, with safety warnings regarding flash floods and weather conditions.
  In theory, you could do this in a day. But in order to enjoy it you’ll want to request a (difficult to get) overnight backpacking permit and make it a multi-day trip. Plan for a pick-up at White House unless you’re doing a round trip. To be clear, Buckskin Gulch is only 13 miles long, but it ends at the Paria River, with no vehicle access. From the river you’ll need to hike another 10 miles to get to the White House Trailhead. **Side note**: This section at the confluence of the Paria River is a great place to camp if you’ve secured a permit. Serious backpackers can travel **Paria Canyon to Lees Ferry** – taking 3-5 days. While an unbelievably amazing journey, we see over and over again that Buckskin Gulch is the most enjoyable segment. This post does NOT cover the rappelling option from Middle Trail or the 23 mile full hike – we are sharing the deets on the 5.6 mile family-friendly day hike. The best way to see the bottom of Buckskin Gulch while hiking through the Paria Narrows to or from the White House Trailhead is to take a side trip directly at the **Buckskin Gulch & Paria River Confluence**. 

Located roughly 7 miles down-canyon from the White House Trailhead, the confluence marks the junction where Buckskin Gulch empties into the Paria River. As detailed by [Bearfoot Theory](w1) and [Halfway Anywhere](w2), you can simply drop your heavy backpack at the confluence—or at one of the elevated campsites nearby—and hike upstream into the mouth of Buckskin Gulch as an out-and-back spur.

### Tips for this side trip:
- **Distance & Timing:** Walking just 15 to 30 minutes up Buckskin Gulch gives you an immediate look at its soaring, razor-thin Navajo sandstone corridors and dark, sculpted narrows, which feel distinctly narrower and more dramatic than the main Paria corridor.
- **Conditions & Obstacles:** The lower end of Buckskin Gulch often harbors muddy sediment, log jams, and standing pools of murky water that can range from ankle- to waist- or chest-deep. Turn around whenever conditions exceed your comfort level.
- **Flash Flood Safety:** Because slot canyons offer virtually no escape routes, only enter Buckskin Gulch if the weather forecast is completely clear across the entire drainage area.

- **Location:** Situated just above the village of Tala, tucked into the hills at the head of a scenic gorge.

**Many Glacier** and the **North Fork** are completely separate, distinct regions located on opposite sides of the Continental Divide, and there is no direct road connecting them inside the park.

### How They Compare:
* **Many Glacier (East Side):** Situated in the northeastern section of the park, Many Glacier is accessed via a dead-end spur road starting outside the park near Babb along US-89. It is celebrated for dramatic alpine valleys, glaciated peaks, and iconic trails around the historic [Many Glacier Hotel](https://osm.org/way/83326064) and Swiftcurrent Lake.
* **North Fork (West Side):** Tucked into the far northwestern corner along the Canadian border, the North Fork is Glacier's most remote vehicle-accessible region. As noted by [Gather and Go Travel](w2), visitors reach it through the Polebridge entrance near the off-grid community of [Polebridge](https://osm.org/node/150971200) and the [Polebridge Ranger Station](https://osm.org/way/83326748). Access requires driving rough, unpaved gravel roads leading to destinations like Bowman Lake and Kintla Lake.

### Traveling Between Them:
Driving between the two requires exiting one area and circumnavigating the park:
1. **Across the Park (Summer only):** Drive south from Babb to St. Mary, take the Going-to-the-Sun Road over Logan Pass to West Glacier, and then head north along North Fork Road / Camas Road to Polebridge (typically 3 to 4+ hours, depending on pass traffic).
2. **Around the Southern Boundary (US-2):** Drive south to East Glacier Park, take US-2 around the southern edge of the park to West Glacier/Columbia Falls, and head north up to Polebridge (about 3.5 to 4.5 hours).

Getting to **Nanstein Castle** (*Burg Nanstein*) in Landstuhl from nearby Ramstein is very quick and straightforward, with several travel options:

### 1. By Car (10–15 minutes)
- Take the **L363** south directly from Ramstein to Landstuhl (roughly 6–7 km). 
- Once in Landstuhl, follow the road signs directing up the hill toward *Burg Nanstein* along *Kirchenstraße* and *Burgweg*.
- A visitor parking lot is situated directly beneath the castle grounds near the on-site restaurant (*Burgschänke Nanstein*).

### 2. By Public Transit (Train or Bus + Walk)
- **Train (RB66):** Take the regional train from **Ramstein station** to **Landstuhl station** (about 6–8 minutes).
- **Bus:** Local buses (such as line 160) also run between Ramstein and Landstuhl Bahnhof.
- **From Landstuhl Station to the Castle:**
  - **On foot (approx. 20–25 minutes):** Walk south from the station through Landstuhl's old town (passing the *Alte Markt* and the historic church), then follow the signposted uphill pedestrian trail along *Burgweg* to the castle gate.
  - **By local bus:** Local buses (e.g., city bus lines from the station to stops like *Landstuhl Burg Nanstein* or *Melkerei*) run up the hillside partway, reducing the uphill walk.

### 3. By Bicycle or Foot (Scenic Option)
- Cyclists can ride the paved cycle paths south through the moorland (*Westpfälzer Moorniederung*) to Landstuhl in about 20–25 minutes, followed by a steep climb up the sandstone ridge to the fortress ruins.

Dharamkot does not have its own railway station due to its high-altitude Himalayan terrain. The closest major broad-gauge railway hub is **Pathankot** (specifically **Pathankot Cantonment** or **Pathankot Junction** in Punjab).

### 1. Train Leg: Delhi to Pathankot
From Delhi, the most convenient train routes run along the Northern Railway mainline toward Jammu:
- **Fastest Daytime Train:** The **Vande Bharat Express** (from New Delhi Railway Station to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra) stops at Pathankot Cantonment (`PTKC`), covering the journey in about 6 hours.
- **Overnight Trains:** As noted by [Global Gallivanting](w1) and [Drifter Planet](w2), an overnight sleeper train is a favorite among travelers. Popular daily options include the **Dhauladhar Express** (running directly to Pathankot Junction, `PTK`) or the **Jammu Mail** and **Uttar Sampark Kranti** (stopping at Pathankot Cantt). An overnight sleeper departs late in the evening and drops you off early the next morning.

### 2. Road Leg: Pathankot to Dharamkot
From Pathankot, you continue up into the Kangra Valley:
- **Taxi:** A direct cab from Pathankot station directly to Dharamkot takes roughly 2.5 to 3 hours, as highlighted by [Drifter Planet](w3).
- **Bus & Local Transit:** State and local buses run frequently from Pathankot bus stand to Dharamshala or McLeod Ganj (about 3.5 to 4.5 hours). From McLeod Ganj's main bus stand, you can take a 10-minute auto-rickshaw or taxi up to Dharamkot, or make the scenic 20-minute uphill walk.

[w1] Dharamkot Guide: A Hippie Village in the Indian Himalayas — global-gallivanting.com
  Recommended restaurants in Dharamkot, Bhagsu, and McLeod Ganj, along with transportation options from major Indian cities and local transit to the village.
  My favourite places to eat in Dharamkot where **Trek and Dine, Om Café and Spaced Out** (good for gluten free and vegan food) **Once in Nature **and** Cool Talk Cafe. **I also had breakfast in the **chai shop outside Tushita** every morning after meditation as its probably the cheapest place and always lively with a nice crowd after meditation. In Bhagsu I recommend **the German Bakery** (the original one further up the hill) and **Unity Café. **In McLeod Ganj try** Tibet Kitchen **in the main square for tasty authentic Tibetan food. ## Getting to Dharamkot I went to Dharamkot from Amritsar (well worth checking out the amazing Golden Temple) via Pathankot on local bus and it took pretty much all day. You can get delux overnight buses to Dharamsala and McLeod Ganj from Delhi. You can also get a bus from Kasol (Parvati Valley) and Manali and other popular Himachal destinations. Another option is to take an overnight train from Delhi to **Pathankot station**. From Pathankot you can take a local bus (4/5 hours) or taxi (2.5 hours) to McLeod Ganj. From McLeod Ganj bus station you can take an auto rickshaw up to Dharamkot or walk via a short cut in about 20 mins. Dharamkot is connected to Upper Bhagsu (the good bit) by a nice 15 min walk down the mountains and I found myself climbing up and down most days going from one workshop to another
[w2] Trekking to Triund in Himachal Pradesh, India — drifterplanet.com
  Options for traveling from Delhi to McLeodganj include an overnight AC Volvo bus or an overnight train to Pathankot, with a scenic narrow-gauge train ride available as an alternative.
  Book an AC Volvo bus and carry a blanket. All the other options suck! These buses depart e very few hours from 4 pm to 7 pm from ISBT that’s near Majnu ka Tila. This journey will cost you around Rs. 1000 to Rs. 1300 per person. Being train obsessed, I prefer the second alternative. For this, you can take an overnight train from Delhi to Pathankot. From Pathankot, you can take a local bus to MacLeoganj. If you have a little time on your hand, there is a narrow gauge train journey from Pathankot to the lovely Kangra Valley that you can do.
[w3] Dharamkot - a Hippie village in the Himalayas (Himachal Pradesh), India
  Travel options from Pathankot and Delhi to Dharamkot, including taxi, bus, and auto-rickshaw details from McLeodganj.
  I love to sleep! There are two options to reach Dharamkot from Pathankot – take a taxi to Dharamkot or a local bus to McLeodganj. The taxi takes around 2.5 hours depending on the traffic and the buses take 4 to 5 hours since they stop at many villages to pick up people and make more money. I have traveled by both. If you decide to travel by a local bus, it will most likely drop you in McLeodganj, not Dharamkot. You can walk to Dharamkot in 20 minutes from McLeodganj or just take an auto-rickshaw or a taxi. to I have been to McLeodganj a few times while I was a student, so I usually skip this place all together because it has become extremely crowded and is no longer a backpacker destination. ### Reaching Dharamkot by Bus from Delhi It is very easy to reach Dharamkot by bus. You can also take a direct overnight bus from Delhi to McLeodganj. A decent bus will cost you around INR 1000 – 1200 per person but I prefer the trains. ### McLeodganj to Dharamkot From McLeodganj bus stop, there’s a short cut to Dharamkot which will take you 15 minutes to cover if you walk at a leisurely pace, and 20 if you’re carrying luggage and are tired from a bumpy butt breaking bus journey from Pathankot. Ask anyone at the bus station to point you to the right direction since most of the people here understand English. Upon reaching Dharamkot, you can replenish your energy at any one of the beautiful cafes. I have never had a bad meal or a bad cup of coffee or tea in this area.
[w4] Old Manali VS Kasol VS Dharamkot: Which Hippy Tourist Town in India is Right for You? - Jonistravell
  Exploring Dharamkot, Himachal Pradesh, including its spiritual atmosphere, nearby waterfall hike, and transport options from Delhi.
  I boldly went where dozens, possibly hundreds, of travel bloggers have already been in an attempt to find out. ## Dharamkot I arrived in Dharamkot armed with some valuable inside knowledge in the form of James, an Australian artist I’d met on the bus who has been visiting India on and off for the last couple of decades. We then met another Australian, Mitch, and spent many an hour hanging out on the deck outside our rooms. From there we could see a constant stream of people eating and drinking in the restaurant downstairs or simply passing by us on the rocky path below. Everybody seems to be either constantly stoned and / or obsessed with doing yoga / some form of new age healing in Dharamkot. The Dalai Lama’s residence is a short walk away in McLeod Ganj and spiritual travellers are drawn to him like magnets to metal (or is it metal to magnets?). I was pretty lazy in Dharamkot, but I did manage to hike to a waterfall outside of town. It was a pleasant, and in some places treacherous, walk but the word waterfall may have been mistranslated. It’s basically a few pools full of clear green water — it’s actually really nice but don’t go there expecting thunderous cascades. I had planned to hike up to Triund, which is one of the better hikes in this area, but I was too lazy — it seems like it’s worth doing though. ## Getting there / Where to Stay You can get to Mcleod Ganj from Delhi on an overnight bus. It takes around 12 hours and is pretty comfortable (I did this journey in the opposite direction, from Mcleod Ganj to Delhi).

Dharamkot does not have its own railway station due to its high-altitude Himalayan terrain. The closest major broad-gauge railway hub is **Pathankot** (specifically **Pathankot Cantonment** or **Pathankot Junction** in Punjab).

### 1. Train Leg: Delhi to Pathankot
From Delhi, the most convenient train routes run along the Northern Railway mainline toward Jammu:
- **Fastest Daytime Train:** The **Vande Bharat Express** (from New Delhi Railway Station to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra) stops at Pathankot Cantonment (`PTKC`), covering the journey in about 6 hours.
- **Overnight Trains:** As noted by [Global Gallivanting](w1) and [Drifter Planet](w2), an overnight sleeper train is a favorite among travelers. Popular daily options include the **Dhauladhar Express** (running directly to Pathankot Junction, `PTK`) or the **Jammu Mail** and **Uttar Sampark Kranti** (stopping at Pathankot Cantt). An overnight sleeper departs late in the evening and drops you off early the next morning.

### 2. Road Leg: Pathankot to Dharamkot
From Pathankot, you continue up into the Kangra Valley:
- **Taxi:** A direct cab from Pathankot station directly to Dharamkot takes roughly 2.5 to 3 hours, as highlighted by [Drifter Planet](w3).
- **Bus & Local Transit:** State and local buses run frequently from Pathankot bus stand to Dharamshala or McLeod Ganj (about 3.5 to 4.5 hours). From McLeod Ganj's main bus stand, you can take a 10-minute auto-rickshaw or taxi up to Dharamkot, or make the scenic 20-minute uphill walk.

[w1] Information about the ferry Tromso - Lyngen Alps (Breivikeidet - Svensby)
  Travelers do not need to book the Breivikeidet to Svensby ferry in advance, though arriving 45 minutes early is recommended during peak times.
  Why? I don’t know 😀 In the following blogpost, I explain you how to get the *toll tag for Norway* and how to have huge discounts on ferries. ## Do I need to book the ferry in advance? No, **you can’t book in advance**. You have to arrive earlier, but frankly not much earlier (unless it’s Friday afternoon or Saturday morning, I’d say allow 45 minutes in advance, especially in summer).
[w2] A day in Skerries — Shetland With Laurie
  Booking the Skerries ferry from Vidlin and experiencing the scenic, potentially bumpy crossing to the Shetland islands.
  * Book the Skerries ferry by calling the Ulsta Booking Office on +44(0) 1595745804 or visit the Shetland Ferries website at https://www.shetland.gov.uk/ferries/ferry-booking for more information. The ferry crossing is one of the longer ferry journeys you can take in Shetland, although Fair Isle and Foula are longer, and we travelled in on the *Fivla* – the usual Skerries ferry, *Filla*, was getting a refit when we travelled, so the fleet’s standby ferry was operating the route. Once onboard, we were invited into the wheelhouse where the captain, Ivan Reid, showed us around the bridge and entrusted us with steering the vessel – apologies if you were onboard when we made a somewhat ‘wiggly’ passage around Skerries towards the harbour. The view from the bridge was fantastic, and as we watched the low-lying hills of Shetland disappear, the cluster of islands that make up the Skerries came into view on the eastern horizon. Away from the shelter of the land, it was easy to see why this could be a notoriously bumpy crossing in the winter months.

And a live map of our current route and most recent log entries always is available at mvdirona.com/maps. |

  The ferry between Breivikeidet and Svensby does not require advance reservations, though arriving 45 minutes early is recommended during peak summer weekends.
  ¿Por qué? No lo sé 😀 ## ¿Tengo que reservar el ferry con antelación? No, **no se puede reservar** con antelación. Hay que llegar antes, pero francamente no mucho antes (a menos que sea viernes por la tarde o sábado por la mañana, yo diría que con 45 minutos de antelación, sobre todo en verano). Hay sitio de sobra, con una veintena de coches fáciles que pueden entrar en el ferry, junto con transportes o autobuses turísticos.
[w5] Havøysund Travel Guide: What to Know Before Visiting — meganstarr.com
  Getting to Havøysund, Norway, by driving the 67 km scenic route from Kokelv or taking the Hurtigruten.
  Today, Havøysund is one of the stops on the Hurtigruten. It is the last stop before reaching Honningsvåg, where you can get off and head to the North Cape. There is not much happening here, but perhaps it is just perfect that way. ## How to Get to Havøysund Getting to Havøysund is half the fun! If you’re coming from the Hurtigruten, you can simply disembark here with your ticket. Alternatively, you can fly to Lakselv (LKL), the closest airport, which is around 104 km (65 mi) from Havøysund. However, the best way to get to Havøysund is by driving (in summer). Havøysund sits at the end of one of Norway’s famous scenic routes and is said to be the northernmost scenic route in the world. The Havøysund Nasjonal Turistveg (Havøysund National Tourist Route) is 67 kilometers long (41.5 miles) and goes from Kokelv village north to Havøysund. It winds around sea cliffs, through fjords, and over mountain plateaus where you’ll share the road with reindeer. It passes other small villages along the way, like Snefjord, where you can stop and relax at one of the rest shelters near the sea. Havøysund is also a launchpad for some of the islands in the north, like Måsøya, Rolvsøya, and Ingøya. You’re also not far from Hjelmsøya, one of Europe’s most important bird cliffs, but you can only reach it by private boat, so it is not easy to access. The other three aforementioned islands all have ferries (although you will need to call for the Måsøya one). While this drive is epic during the summer months, it will require a convoy (kolonnekjøring) in the winter months.

The Clink is located at HMP Cardiff. Yes, you read that correct, this fine dining restaurant is located in the grounds of Cardiff Prison and run by prisoners who are working towards qualifications in catering and cookery. The leather upholstery and boardroom tables used in the restaurant are made by prisoners at HMP Frankland, and the poetry on display is from former Clink trainees. Clink’s menu uses only local and seasonal Welsh produce, and you can sample the likes of Cawl, a Welsh stew made with Welsh Lamb. Now one of the top Cardiff attractions, the project has been such a success in reducing re-offending rates and preparing prisoners for life outside, that three other Clink restaurants have opened at HMP Brixton, HMP High Down and HMP Styal. ### Chippy Lane If you’re planning on partying at night in one of Cardiff’s many cocktail bars, happy hour venues or nightclubs then the only way to end the night is on Caroline Street.
